title: The 1/25th Second
hook: A feeling can cross a face in a twenty-fifth of a second and vanish; the skill is not catching the flash but knowing how little it proves.
why:
Few ideas about body language are as famous as the microexpression: a flash of true feeling that crosses the face too fast for the person to stop it, there and gone before anyone notices. Television dramas built whole series on it. Training courses promise to teach it in an afternoon. Some of it is real. Brief, partial expressions do happen, and with practice you can learn to see more of them.

What the legend leaves out is how rare full microexpressions are, how many brief movements of the face have nothing to do with hidden feeling, and how little a flash can tell you even when you see it clearly. This chapter takes the idea apart and keeps the useful pieces. You will learn where the idea came from, what the research has found about how often and how fast these expressions occur, what else makes faces flicker, what training can and cannot do, and how to treat a flash as what it is: a moment worth noting, and a reason to ask, never a verdict about what someone feels.

teach.h: The flash was found in slow motion.
teach.p:
The idea began with film. In 1966 the psychologists Ernest Haggard and Kenneth Isaacs described what they called micromomentary expressions. Running films of psychotherapy sessions at slow speed, they saw changes of expression that lasted only a few frames and that nobody had noticed at normal speed, including the therapists who had been in the room.

A few years later Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen reported a case that made the idea famous. They studied a film of an interview with a woman in psychiatric care whose cheerful manner had persuaded her doctors that she was recovering. Slowed down frame by frame, the film showed brief moments in which her face registered anguish before the smile returned. Ekman and Friesen called such moments micro expressions and described them as leakage of a feeling the person was trying to hide, a theme the chapter on leakage and pacifiers develops.

Notice how these discoveries were made. In each case the flash was found afterwards, on film, by researchers who could replay the same seconds again and again, and who already knew how the story had turned out. Nobody in the room saw it at the time.

That is not a reason to dismiss the idea. It is a reason to be precise about what it offers. A microexpression is something that can be seen on careful review, sometimes. Whether it can be seen reliably in real time, and what it means when it is, are separate questions, and the rest of this chapter takes them one at a time.

Start from the honest picture: a real phenomenon, found in slow motion, and inflated in the telling.
teach.disconfirm: If you find that you can reliably see brief expressions in live conversation that you later confirm on recordings of the same moments, real-time spotting is more within your reach than this block suggests. Check it with a willing friend and a camera before trusting it.

teach.h: What a microexpression is, and how fast.
teach.p:
An ordinary facial expression, which researchers sometimes call a macroexpression, usually lasts somewhere between half a second and several seconds, and often involves several parts of the face at once. A microexpression is the same kind of movement compressed into a fraction of a second, too brief to register as a deliberate display.

The title of this chapter comes from Ekman's description of microexpressions lasting as little as a twenty-fifth of a second. Later measurements suggest a somewhat wider range. In 2013 Wen-Jing Yan, Xiaolan Fu and colleagues filmed people trying to keep a straight face while watching emotional clips, and measured the brief expressions that escaped. Most lasted under half a second from start to finish, which is now a common working definition.

Three variants are worth knowing. A full microexpression involves the whole configuration of a feeling, brows, eyes and mouth together, compressed in time. A partial one involves only one region: a brow pinch, a lip press, a flicker at the nose. And a squelched expression is one that starts and is then cut off and covered, often by a smile, so that what you see is the start of one feeling and the end of another.

In practice, almost everything you will ever see is partial or squelched. The full flash of the textbook plate is the rarest of the three.

This matters for how you watch. If you are looking for a whole face of fear or anger, you will mostly see nothing. If you are looking for a single region moving briefly and then stopping, you will see a great deal, and most of it will need a careful explanation that has nothing to do with hidden feeling.
teach.disconfirm: If careful frame-by-frame review of ordinary conversations regularly showed full-face expressions lasting under half a second, the claim that partial flashes are far more common would be wrong. Count the full and partial flashes in ten minutes of slowed recording before forming a view.

teach.h: They are rarer than the legend says.
teach.p:
In 2008 Stephen Porter and Leanne ten Brinke tested the legend directly. They showed participants disturbing, sad, frightening and happy images, and asked them sometimes to show their genuine reaction and sometimes to show a false one: to look happy at a disturbing image, for example, or to keep a neutral face. Then they coded nearly seven hundred expressions, frame by frame, from the recordings.

Microexpressions were rare. Only a small fraction of the expressions contained one, and none of them involved the whole face; each appeared in either the upper or the lower half only. They appeared in roughly a fifth of the participants, which means that most people never showed one at all. And they appeared in genuine expressions as well as false ones.

Porter and ten Brinke also found that false expressions often leaked in other, less dramatic ways, with inconsistent or partial movements, and that some kinds of concealment leaked more than others. So the idea that the face betrays effort is not empty. But the particular picture of a full, telltale flash that reveals a hidden feeling every time someone conceals one did not survive.

For a reader, the practical consequences are two. First, the absence of a flash means very little; most people concealing something will show none. Second, the presence of a flash means less than it seems, because the same brief movement turned up when people were not concealing anything.

Treat every flash, then, as one data point in a cluster, never as a conclusion in itself.
teach.disconfirm: If later, larger studies found that full microexpressions appear in most people who conceal a feeling and rarely in people who do not, this block would need revising. As of the research it describes, the evidence points the other way.
teach.pullQuote: The absence of a flash means very little, and its presence means less than it seems.

teach.p:
Watch any face at slow speed and you will find it moving almost constantly. Most of that movement has nothing to do with emotion, and a reader who has not learned the ordinary sources of facial movement will see hidden feelings everywhere.

Speech is the first source. The lips, jaw and cheeks move with every sound, and some sounds pull the mouth into shapes that, frozen in a single frame, look like contempt or disgust. Blinks, swallows and small adjustments to the jaw are constant. Many people have habitual movements, a sniff, a lip bite, a brief grimace, that appear dozens of times an hour regardless of topic.

Effort is the second. When people think hard, recalling a date, working out a figure, choosing a word, their brows often lower and draw together for a moment. Studies that measure the muscle activity above the brow have found that it rises with mental effort as well as with negative feeling. The brief frown of a colleague asked about a deadline may be anger. It may just as well be arithmetic.

The third is the body's own reactions. A flash of light, a sudden noise, a twinge of pain or a smell in the room will move a face as fast as any concealed feeling.

This is why the baseline comes first, even for the face. Before you can say that a flash was unusual, you need to know what this face does while this person talks, thinks and listens. A man who frowns briefly every time he does sums is telling you he is doing sums.
teach.disconfirm: If, after building a baseline for someone's ordinary speaking, thinking and listening face, you still see brief movements that fit none of those patterns and recur at the same kind of moment, you have something worth noting. Without the baseline, you cannot tell.

teach.h: Your brain sees more than you notice.
teach.p:
You may not consciously see a flash, and yet it may still reach you. In 1998 Paul Whalen and colleagues showed people pictures of fearful and happy faces for about a thirtieth of a second, each immediately followed by a neutral face that masked it. Participants said they had seen only the neutral faces. Yet brain scans showed that the amygdala, a region involved in detecting threat, responded more to the hidden fearful faces than to the hidden happy ones.

Findings like this help explain a common experience: you leave a conversation with a sense that something was off, without being able to say what. Part of your perception may have registered a brief change that never reached awareness, or a mismatch between channels that the chapter on clusters and congruence will help you name.

That feeling is worth taking seriously, and worth distrusting at the same time. It may rest on something real. It may also rest on your own mood, your expectations, or a stereotype about the person, all of which can produce exactly the same sense of unease. A gut feeling does not come labelled with its source.

The useful response is to treat the feeling as a pointer. Ask yourself when it started and what was being said at the time. If you can find the moment, look again at the next similar moment, or replay a recording if you have one. If you cannot find any moment at all, the feeling may be about you rather than them.

A hunch is where looking begins. It is never where looking ends.
teach.disconfirm: If your unexplained sense that something was off in a conversation turns out, when you check, to be no more often right than wrong, the hunch is not tracking anything in the other person. Log the hunches for a month, with outcomes, before trusting them.

teach.h: Training sharpens the eye, not the judgment.
teach.p:
Can people learn to see brief expressions? Yes, to a degree. Ekman developed a training tool that flashes faces on a screen and gives immediate feedback, and studies of it and similar tools, including one by David Matsumoto and Hyi Sung Hwang in 2011, found that people's accuracy at recognising brief expressions improved after short training and stayed improved for some weeks.

Notice what was measured. The training improved people's ability to name the expression in a brief, posed, isolated face shown on a screen, in a test built from the same kind of faces. That is a real perceptual skill, and it may help you notice more. There is much less evidence that it makes people better at judging what others feel or intend in ordinary conversation, where faces move constantly, expressions are partial, and context changes everything. Whether training helps anyone detect lies is a separate question, which the chapter on deception answers plainly.

The most useful practice is humbler than any course. Take a recorded public interview and watch it at a quarter of normal speed. Each time a region of the face moves briefly and stops, write down the time and describe the movement, not the emotion: brows lowered and drawn together, lips pressed, one corner of the mouth tucked in. Then write what was being said at that moment, and two or three possible causes.

Done regularly, this trains your eye to notice and your mind to describe before interpreting. That second habit is worth more than the first.

See more. Conclude less.
teach.disconfirm: If people trained to spot brief expressions turned out, in tests with real conversations and known outcomes, to judge others' feelings much better than untrained people, this block would be too cautious. The evidence it describes does not show that.

teach.h: A flash is a moment, not a message.
teach.p:
Suppose you do see something: a brief tightening of the lips as you mention a price, a flicker of the brows as you name a colleague. What now?

First, note the moment, not the meaning. What exactly had just been said or done? The timing is the most useful thing a flash gives you, because it points to a topic, a word or a person that may matter to the other person in some way you do not yet understand.

Second, look for company. A single brief movement is weak evidence. Does anything else change at the same moment: the voice, the hands, the posture, the words? A flash that arrives with other changes is worth more than one that arrives alone.

Third, if it seems to matter, ask, later and gently, about the topic, never about the face. *How does the price sit with you?* is a reasonable question. *I saw that* is not. Telling someone that you caught a flicker on their face turns a conversation into an inspection, and the person is entitled to resent it, especially since you may well be wrong.

And remember that your own face does the same. When you hear something you did not expect, your face will move before you can decide what to show, and the people you are with may notice. The chapter on video review of yourself, in Part VI, offers a way to see your own flashes. It is a humbling exercise, and it makes you a fairer reader of everyone else.

A flash tells you when to look. It never tells you what you have found.
teach.disconfirm: If asking gently about the topics that coincided with brief facial changes turned up nothing of interest, time after time, compared with asking about other topics, the timing of flashes would not be a useful pointer for you. Keep a short record of a dozen such questions before deciding.
teach.pullQuote: A flash tells you when to look. It never tells you what you have found.

poseGallery.doCaption: Listening normally, and noting when something crossed it.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Staring at a face, waiting for it to slip.
poseGallery.annotation: Staring makes people self-conscious and adds movements of its own. Ordinary attention catches the moment that matters.

poseGallery.doCaption: Asking later, about the topic, not the face.
poseGallery.annotation: A flash points to a moment, not a meaning. Asking about the subject lets the person explain without being inspected.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Trained on flashcards, now sure of every face.
poseGallery.annotation: Training improves recognition of brief posed faces. It does not make a flash in real conversation mean any more than it does.

poseGallery.doCaption: Ten minutes, naming movements before meanings.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Hours of slowed footage, hunting for tells.
poseGallery.annotation: Describing the movement first, and its possible causes second, is the habit that slow-motion practice should build.

caseStudy:
Jonah, thirty-four, an account manager, has spent a few evenings watching online videos about microexpressions, and goes into a pitch feeling sharper than usual. Halfway through, as he explains the delivery timeline, the client's operations director, Eleanor, shows a brief frown and a press of the lips. It is gone in an instant. Jonah is certain he has seen her reject the timeline.

He spends the rest of the meeting reassuring her about deadlines she has not questioned, and that evening rewrites the proposal with a shorter schedule his team cannot meet. His manager, Priti, asks what Eleanor actually said about the timeline. Nothing, Jonah admits. He saw it on her face.

Priti suggests he ask. The next morning he emails Eleanor a short note asking whether the proposed schedule works for her side. Eleanor replies that the timeline is fine. She had been working out in her head whether the second phase would land in the week her warehouse closes for stocktaking, which it does, by two days. Could they move that phase back a week?

The frown had been arithmetic. The press of the lips had been the moment she found the clash. Jonah had seen something real, at a real moment, and had attached the wrong meaning to it, then acted on the meaning instead of asking about the moment.

He puts the original schedule back, moves the second phase by a week, and writes in his journal: *saw a flash at the timeline; it pointed to something; it did not tell me what.* At the next pitch he notices a similar flicker when he mentions training. This time he asks, at the end, how the training plan looks to them, and learns about a shift pattern he had not known existed.
observe: Watch two minutes of a recorded public interview at a quarter of normal speed, and note every brief movement of the brows or mouth that you did not see at normal speed.
In conversation this week, notice one moment when a face seemed to change too quickly to name, and note what had just been said.
On your next video call, glance at your own image when someone says something unexpected, and notice how fast your face moves before you decide what to show.

drills.name: Quarter Speed
steps: Choose a recorded interview of someone answering unscripted questions, at least five minutes long.
Watch it once at normal speed and note any changes of expression you see.
Watch it again at a quarter of normal speed and note every brief movement of a single region of the face, with the time.
Describe each movement in plain words, such as brows lowered and drawn together, without naming an emotion.
Compare the two lists and count how many movements you missed at normal speed.

drills.name: Movement, Not Meaning
steps: Open the face plates in the pose library and, for each face, say aloud which parts of the face have moved.
Return to your slowed recording and choose five brief movements from your list.
For each, write three possible causes, at least one of which has nothing to do with emotion, such as effort, speech or light.
Note what was being said at the moment of each movement.
Mark any movement that coincided with a change in voice, hands or posture as well.

drills.name: The Effort Face
steps: Ask a willing friend to answer a few easy questions and then a few hard ones, such as multiplying seventeen by twenty-four in their head.
Watch their brows, lids and mouth as they answer each kind of question.
Note the movements that appear only with the hard questions.
Swap roles and ask your friend what they saw on your face.
Write down your friend's effort face and your own, as a baseline for later.

drills.name: Moment Log
steps: For one week, whenever you notice a face change briefly in conversation, write down the moment afterwards.
Record what had just been said or done, and anything else that changed at the same time.
Write your first guess at the cause, and one rival.
Note what you did, if anything, and whether you later learned more.
At the end of the week, count how many guesses you could check and how many held up.

drills.name: Your Own Flash
steps: With a friend's agreement, record a short video call in which they tell you something surprising they have prepared in advance.
Watch your own face at a quarter speed at the moment of the surprise.
Note what moved, how long it lasted, and whether you were aware of it at the time.
Ask your friend whether they noticed it live.
Delete the recording once you have made your notes.

quiz.q: A colleague's brows lower and her lips press for an instant when she hears the new deadline. What does that flash tell you?
options: That she is angry about the deadline and is trying to hide it from you
That she disagrees, and will not support the plan when it really matters
That something registered at that moment, cause unknown, worth a gentle question
That she is lying when she says she is happy with the plan you proposed
quiz.explain: A brief brow lowering and lip press can come from effort, doubt, discomfort or a sudden thought about something else. The flash marks a moment worth asking about. It does not tell you what the moment meant.

quiz.q: What did Porter and ten Brinke find when they coded nearly seven hundred expressions frame by frame?
options: They were rare, partial, and appeared in genuine expressions too
They appeared in almost every false expression that they examined
They were full-face expressions lasting a second or two each time
They appeared only in people who had been trained to hide feelings
quiz.explain: Microexpressions turned up in only a small fraction of expressions, never across the whole face, and in genuine as well as false ones. Most people never showed one at all.

quiz.q: By most current definitions, roughly how long does a microexpression last?
options: Between two and five seconds, like an ordinary expression of feeling
Exactly one twenty-fifth of a second, in every person and situation
Longer than a second, but only ever on the lower half of the face
Under half a second, sometimes as little as a twenty-fifth
quiz.explain: Ekman described flashes as brief as a twenty-fifth of a second, and later measurements suggest most last under half a second in all. Ordinary expressions usually last from half a second to several seconds.

quiz.q: A friend has done an online microexpression course and says he can now tell what anyone really feels. What fits this chapter?
options: Agree, since this kind of training is proven to improve real-life readings
Training sharpens spotting brief faces, not judging what people feel
Suggest he use it to test whether his partner is being honest with him
Tell him microexpressions do not exist and the course was a complete waste
quiz.explain: Studies find training improves recognition of brief posed faces on a screen. There is much less evidence that it improves judgments of real people in real conversations, and none that it licenses testing a partner.

quiz.q: What did Whalen and colleagues find when fearful faces were flashed too briefly for people to report seeing them?
options: People reported every fearful face they had been shown, despite the mask
The brain's response was identical for the fearful and the happy faces
The amygdala responded more to them, though people said they saw nothing
People became anxious only if they had been told what to look for
quiz.explain: Part of perception registers brief faces that never reach awareness. That can explain a vague sense that something was off, but the same sense can also come from your own mood or expectations, so it is a reason to look again, not a conclusion.

quiz.q: In a meeting you see a client's lips press for an instant as you mention the price. What is the best next step?
options: Note the moment, and later ask an open question about the price
Lower the price straight away, before the objection has a chance to harden
Tell the client you noticed a reaction, so that it is out in the open
Ignore it entirely, since brief movements of the face never mean anything
quiz.explain: The flash gives you a moment, the price, and nothing more. Asking about the topic later lets the client tell you what, if anything, it meant, without being told their face was being watched.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific moment when you were sure you saw what someone really felt in a brief change of their face. What exactly did you see, and what had just been said? What did you conclude, and what did you do? Looking back with what this chapter says about effort, speech and how rare full flashes are, list two other explanations for the same movement. What would you do differently if you saw it again tomorrow?
reflection.guidance: Most people find their example in an argument, a negotiation or a moment of bad news, where they were primed to see a reaction. Try to describe the movement itself before the meaning you gave it. If you acted on the reading without asking, notice how the story might have gone if you had asked about the moment instead.

failureMode: The commonest failure is to become a hunter of tells: staring at faces, waiting for them to slip, and treating every brief movement as a confession. It makes conversations stiff, adds movements of its own, and fills your head with confident misreadings. A second failure is overconfidence after training, believing that recognising flashed faces on a screen means you can read hidden feelings in real people. A third is forgetting the ordinary sources of facial movement, so that a frown of arithmetic is read as anger and a speech sound as contempt. The most damaging is to confront people with what you think their face showed. Note the moment, look for company, and ask about the topic if it matters.
